subtitle: Design program integrity reviews that prevent and address fraud while staying proportionate. You will learn to avoid profiling, protect due process and continuity of care, and communicate accurately.
audience: For DHS program integrity leaders and staff, DSD program and policy leaders who work with oversight, supervisors of review and audit teams, and facilitators who support fair enforcement design.

lessons.title: Two kinds of harm: fraud and careless enforcement
objectives: Explain how fraud harms people who rely on public programs, not only public budgets.
Identify ways that poorly designed enforcement can harm people served, honest providers and communities.
Distinguish fraud from other improper payments such as errors and documentation gaps.
Describe the four components of the GAO Fraud Risk Management Framework.
lessons.teaching:
Program integrity leaders hold two responsibilities at once. Fraud in human services programs is real and it hurts people. When a provider bills for services never delivered, the person who needed those services goes without, public trust erodes, and money that could have supported others is lost. Some schemes also exploit the people enrolled, using their identities or cutting their care. DHS has publicly described a stronger program integrity effort under its Office of Inspector General, including heightened scrutiny of services it has designated as high risk, revalidation of providers, pauses on new enrollment in some services, payment withholds and third-party billing reviews. Leaders in this work need to take fraud seriously.

Careless enforcement also causes harm. An enforcement action against a provider can abruptly end services for people who had nothing to do with any wrongdoing. Broad sweeps can burden honest small providers with demands they have limited staff or resources to meet. Reviewers should examine how those demands affect providers and the people they serve, including immigrant, Black, Indigenous and disabled communities, without assuming that every organization has the same experience. Public statements that link a community to fraud can stigmatize people who receive services lawfully and discourage eligible families from seeking help. Mistaken findings, when they happen, cost people money, reputation and care. Oversight should address fraud while examining and limiting avoidable harm.

A first discipline is precise language. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services treats improper payments and fraud as related but distinct. An improper payment can come from an error, a missing signature, a misunderstanding of a rule or a system problem. Fraud involves intentional deception. Waste and abuse are different again. Treating every error as fraud leads to disproportionate responses and poisons relationships with providers who could have fixed a problem with guidance.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office Fraud Risk Management Framework gives leaders a structure. It has four components: commit to combating fraud by creating a culture and structure for managing fraud risk; assess by planning regular fraud risk assessments and building a risk profile; design and implement a strategy with specific control activities; and evaluate outcomes and adapt. The framework emphasizes prevention and asks managers to set a fraud risk tolerance. It openly acknowledges that managers may weigh the program's mission, such as getting help to people quickly, against lowering the likelihood of fraud. This federal framework offers a planning approach; it does not authorize DHS staff to disregard a required referral, suspension or other duty. Confirm those obligations through the person or area responsible.
lessons.keyPoint: Fraud harms people and so can careless enforcement. Use precise terms (error, improper payment, fraud) and a structured approach such as the GAO framework that weighs program mission alongside fraud risk.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: A program integrity unit finds that a group of providers in one service have claims with missing documentation. A team member, Ryan, drafts a memo describing the findings as a fraud problem in that service and suggests immediate payment withholds across the group. His manager, Selam, notices that the documentation rule changed recently and several providers asked for guidance that was never sent.
lessons.question: What should Selam do?
choices: Approve the memo, since strong language will deter wrongdoing across the service.

Separate the findings into possible errors and possible fraud indicators, send guidance where confusion is likely, and refer concerns through the required investigative process without treating a documentation gap as proof of fraud.
Drop the review, because the rule change means nobody can be held accountable.
feedback: Labeling documentation gaps as fraud without evidence of intent is inaccurate and can trigger harmful, disproportionate responses against providers and the people they serve.

This is the strongest response. It uses precise categories, addresses possible confusion and preserves required referral and investigation. The fictional case does not establish whether fraud occurred.
Errors still need correction and recovery where appropriate, and a rule change does not rule out fraud. Dropping the review abandons both responsibilities.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider how you and your colleagues use the word fraud. Where might a more precise term change how a finding is handled?
lessons.action: Use the fictional case or an approved, nonconfidential example to distinguish a documentation gap, a possible explanation and an indicator requiring follow-up. Describe what remains unknown and which role would decide the next step. Keep case, client and investigation records out of learning notes; actual reporting duties follow the designated process.

check.question: Which list gives the four components of the GAO Fraud Risk Management Framework?
check.correct: Commit, assess, design and implement, evaluate and adapt.
check.feedback: The GAO framework moves from creating a culture and structure (commit) through risk assessment, designing and implementing controls with an emphasis on prevention, and evaluating and adapting. Investigation and recovery are parts of a response, not the whole framework.

lessons.title: Proportionate reviews that target conduct, not communities
objectives: Distinguish risk indicators based on conduct or billing patterns from proxies for race, national origin, language or disability.
Explain how federal Title VI rules on selection criteria changed in 2025 and 2026, and why identity-based criteria remain a legal and practical risk.
Plan a tiered set of responses matched to the strength of evidence.
Draft a check that tests review selection criteria for disparate impact before use.
lessons.teaching:
Proportionality means the intensity of an oversight response matches the strength of the evidence and the seriousness of the risk. A tiered approach helps. At the lightest level are education and technical assistance for common errors. Next are targeted reviews of specific claims or records. More serious responses include corrective action plans, recovery of overpayments, payment withholds and referral for investigation or licensing action. Use written criteria and the authority applicable to each response. These examples are not a required sequence: education or further local review must not delay a legally required referral, suspension or other action.

Selection criteria are where profiling can slip in. Useful indicators describe conduct or billing patterns. Examples include hours that exceed a staff member’s available time, services billed during a hospital stay, or claims that do not match approvals. Sudden claim increases or shared addresses may prompt questions, but each pattern needs context and verification. Poor indicators rely on who people are or where they come from: a provider's national origin, the languages spoken by staff, a neighborhood, a faith community or the ethnicity of people served. Even when not intended, indicators like these can become proxies that concentrate scrutiny on particular communities while missing fraud elsewhere.

This is also a legal issue, and the federal position has changed. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act bars intentional discrimination based on race, color or national origin in programs receiving federal funds. A criterion chosen to target people on those grounds can raise that concern directly. Federal regulations also used to bar criteria or methods of administration with discriminatory effects. The Department of Justice removed those provisions effective December 10, 2025 (90 FR 57141), and the Department of Health and Human Services removed its parallel provisions effective July 24, 2026 (FR Doc. 2026-15000). These rules remove the cited effects-based regulatory provisions. Data on unequal outcomes may still be relevant to an inquiry into intentional discrimination. For an actual decision, counsel must confirm current law, court orders and the authorities that apply to the program. The earlier analysis asked three questions. Does the practice cause disproportionate harm? Does a substantial, legitimate need justify it? Could an alternative meet that need with less discrimination? Those questions can still help examine poor targeting. Before using a method, test whether it flags some groups much more often. Check whether flagged patterns predict confirmed problems. Look for effective alternatives that reduce unequal burdens. Whether other federal or Minnesota law applies, and all formal legal conclusions, belong to counsel and the Equal Opportunity and Access Division.

Document the reasons for each selection and each escalation. Documentation protects the integrity of a case, lets supervisors review consistency and makes it possible to learn whether the approach works. With the data owner, review authorized results by relevant provider characteristics and examine whether a pattern may reflect actual risk, selection practices, incomplete information or differences in follow-up. Use appropriate disclosure controls; do not infer identity or collect sensitive information informally for this exercise.
lessons.keyPoint: Match the response to the evidence, select for review based on conduct and billing patterns rather than identity proxies, and test selection criteria for disparate effects before relying on them.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: An analytics team proposes a new rule to flag providers for review. One criterion is that the provider's staff primarily speak a language other than English. The team lead, Hana, asks why it was included. The analyst, Victor, says several past fraud cases involved providers whose staff spoke the same language, so the criterion seemed predictive. The rule is scheduled to go live next week, and Hana has not yet seen any testing of how it performs across provider groups.
lessons.question: What should Hana decide?
choices: Remove the language criterion, replace it with the conduct patterns found in those past cases, and test the revised rule for disparate effects and accuracy before use.
Keep the language criterion because it is based on real past cases.
Keep the criterion but do not document it, so it is not controversial.
feedback: This is the best response. It keeps what was useful in the past cases (the conduct patterns), removes a proxy for national origin, and tests the rule before it is used.

Past cases reflect who was previously looked at as well as who committed fraud. A language criterion targets a community rather than conduct and raises serious civil rights concerns for counsel and EOAD.
Hiding a criterion makes the problem worse. It removes accountability and would be very difficult to defend.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a review or audit process you have seen. Did its selection criteria describe what people did, or who they were? How would you know?
lessons.action: Using the fictional case or approved selection criteria, distinguish a conduct indicator from a possible identity proxy. Draft an alternative and questions about its accuracy and unequal effects. Treat this as a proposal for the responsible review process; the exercise does not authorize changing a live rule.

check.question: Why can a past-case pattern based on a community's language be a poor fraud indicator?
check.correct: Past cases reflect where claims staff previously looked, and the criterion targets identity rather than conduct, which can produce discriminatory effects.
wrong: Because language data is always inaccurate.
Because any criterion that mentions language is automatically unlawful.
check.feedback: Historical enforcement data reflects prior attention as well as actual wrongdoing, and identity-based criteria can concentrate scrutiny on a community. DOJ and HHS removed the effects provisions from their Title VI regulations in 2025 and 2026, so the case for testing here is accuracy and fairness, and legal questions go to counsel and EOAD.

lessons.title: Due process: notice, appeal rights and continuity of care
objectives: Explain the core due process elements recognized in Goldberg v. Kelly.
Identify Medicaid notice and fair hearing protections for people whose services are reduced or ended.
Describe notice requirements and good cause exceptions for provider payment suspensions based on a credible allegation of fraud.
Plan continuity-of-care steps when an oversight action affects people's services.
lessons.teaching:
Due process helps make enforcement legitimate and accurate. In Goldberg v. Kelly, the U.S. Supreme Court required a pre-termination evidentiary hearing for the welfare benefits at issue. The Court required timely notice with reasons and an opportunity to present arguments and evidence and confront adverse witnesses. The decision-maker must be impartial and must not have made the decision under review. The decision should state its reasons and the evidence relied on. These principles inform public-program procedures, but the case does not establish an identical hearing requirement for every benefit or provider action. Apply the rules governing the particular decision.

For people who receive Medicaid, federal fair hearing rules at 42 CFR part 431, subpart E, spell out protections. Notices must state the intended action, effective date, reasons and supporting rules. They must explain hearing rights and when services continue during an appeal. Agencies generally must send notice at least ten days before the action, with limited exceptions, including a shorter period when there are facts indicating probable fraud by the recipient. Under section 431.230, a request before the date of action generally preserves services when the agency sent the required ten-day or five-day notice. An exception applies when the hearing determines that the sole issue is law or policy and the agency gives prompt written notice. If the action is upheld, the rule also allows recovery of service costs in specified circumstances. Confirm the applicable deadlines, continuation rules and hearing route with the responsible appeals staff.

Providers have protections too. Under 42 CFR 455.23, a state Medicaid agency must suspend payments to a provider after determining there is a credible allegation of fraud for which a Medicaid investigation is pending, unless it finds good cause not to suspend or to suspend only in part. Notice generally follows within five days of the action. A written law-enforcement request may delay notice for thirty days and may be renewed twice, up to ninety days total. The notice must state that payments are suspended and describe the general allegations. Specific information about an ongoing investigation need not be disclosed. It must explain the temporary suspension and when it ends, identify affected claims or business units when applicable, and describe the right to submit written evidence. It also must give the applicable state appeal process and legal citations. The good cause provisions include defined risks to access. One concerns a sole community physician or sole source of essential specialized services. Another concerns a provider serving many beneficiaries in a HRSA-designated medically underserved area. HRSA is the federal Health Resources and Services Administration.

That last point connects enforcement to people served. When a withhold, sanction or enrollment action will disrupt services, plan for continuity of care before or alongside the action, where investigative needs allow. Coordinate with counties, Tribal Nations and case managers, and help people find another provider. The people or areas responsible in DHS make formal decisions under applicable authority, with legal counsel advising on legal questions. A suspension based on a credible allegation is not a final fraud finding, and an access concern does not automatically establish an exception.
lessons.keyPoint: Due process makes enforcement fair and accurate: clear notice with reasons, a real chance to respond, an impartial decision and continuity of care. Federal rules include access-based exceptions for provider payment suspensions.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: The Office of Inspector General is preparing a payment withhold against a home care provider based on a credible allegation of fraud. Joy, a DSD program lead, learns the provider is the only agency in two rural counties offering a particular service to several people with high support needs. Her colleague Pete says continuity of care is not their problem because the provider brought the action on itself.
lessons.question: What should Joy do?
choices: Agree with Pete and stay out of the matter, since the withhold is the inspector general's decision.
Contact the provider directly to warn them about the withhold so they can make arrangements for clients.

Share the access information with the responsible OIG staff through proper channels, since federal rules include good cause exceptions tied to beneficiary access, and prepare with counties to support affected people.
feedback: The withhold decision does belong to the person or area responsible, but the people served are DSD's concern, and access information is relevant to a good cause decision.
Warning the provider could compromise an investigation and exceed Joy's authority. Continuity planning must be coordinated with the person or area responsible.
This is the strongest response. It gives decision-makers information federal rules treat as relevant, respects their authority and prepares to protect people's care.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall a notice or decision letter you have seen that left the reader unsure why an action was taken or what they could do. What would clearer due process have looked like?
lessons.action: Use an approved blank notice template or a fictional example. Identify the action, reasons, authority, response or appeal route, deadlines and contact information. Note which continuation rules require confirmation. Share proposed improvements through the template review process; do not paste a real notice or private record into the learning activity.

check.question: Under 42 CFR 455.23, which is a good cause reason a state may decide not to suspend, or only partially suspend, provider payments?
check.correct: Beneficiary access to items or services would be jeopardized by the suspension.
wrong: The provider promises to repay any overpayment later.
The provider is a large organization with many contracts.
check.feedback: The regulation includes specified access grounds: a sole community physician or sole source of essential specialized services, or a provider serving many beneficiaries in a HRSA-designated medically underserved area. Access information must be assessed against the actual rule. Size or a repayment promise alone does not establish those grounds; the person or area responsible determines whether a listed exception applies.

lessons.title: Using data responsibly and communicating with care
objectives: Explain why an analytic flag is a lead for review rather than a finding.
Identify checks that reduce false positives and unequal error rates in data-driven oversight.
Draft public or partner communication about integrity actions that is accurate and avoids stigmatizing communities.
Plan measures that evaluate both fraud prevention and effects on access.
lessons.teaching:
Data analytics can help oversight staff find patterns people would miss, and CMS encourages stronger data use in Medicaid program integrity. But a flag from a data model or query is a lead, not a finding. Data can be wrong: a claim may be coded incorrectly, an authorization may not have loaded, two providers may share an address for innocent reasons such as a shared office building. Before treating a flag as a finding, authorized staff should verify relevant records, consider other explanations and document their reasoning. Follow any required referral or protective action without waiting for a learning exercise. A flag alone does not establish wrongdoing.

Look at error rates, not only hit rates. A review approach can catch real problems and still generate many false positives, and those false positives may fall more heavily on some groups, such as small providers, rural providers or providers serving particular communities. Track the share of completed reviews with confirmed findings, and distinguish unresolved cases from findings ruled out. Compare like periods and review methods where authorized data permits. A low confirmation share calls for investigation of selection, data quality and follow-up; it does not by itself prove that a method has no benefit. That share is not the statistical false-positive rate, which also requires information about cases without the condition of interest. Findings among selected cases cannot establish fraud prevalence across a community. The GAO framework's final component, evaluate and adapt, applies here: measure whether controls work and change them when they do not.

Communication shapes whether integrity work builds or erodes trust. Public statements should describe conduct and actions accurately, avoid implying that a community, language group or faith group is responsible for fraud, and never disclose information protected by data practices law or an ongoing investigation. Coordinate with the DHS communications office and legal counsel before speaking publicly. Messages to people receiving services should be practical: what is happening, whether their services are affected, how to find another provider and who to call. DHS has created public resources to help people find care after service disruptions; point people to official resources rather than improvising.

Finally, measure both sides of the mission. Useful measures include confirmed fraud and recoveries, but also the share of flagged cases confirmed, time to resolve reviews, the number of people whose services were disrupted and how quickly they were reconnected, and appeal outcomes. Interpreting these measures together can help leaders examine both kinds of harm. Explain missing data, pending reviews and limits on comparison. Use authorized summaries and disclosure controls, and provide a clear route for staff to raise concerns about the method.
lessons.keyPoint: Treat data flags as leads to verify, track false positives across groups, communicate about conduct rather than communities, and measure access effects alongside fraud results.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: A data review flags forty providers in one service for unusual billing. Most are small agencies in one metro area serving East African families. A reporter asks the DHS communications office about the review. Min-jun, a program integrity manager, is asked for talking points. So far, staff have verified records for only six of the flagged providers, and two of those had innocent explanations for their billing patterns.
lessons.question: What should Min-jun provide?
choices: Talking points describing a growing fraud problem in the East African provider community, to show DHS is acting.
Accurate talking points about the review process and the conduct it looks for, with no reference to a community and no claim of fraud before verification, and a note that verification is ongoing.
A recommendation to decline all comment and stop the review until public attention fades.
feedback: Linking fraud to a community before verification is inaccurate, stigmatizing and could harm families and honest providers. Two of six verified cases were already explained.
This is the best response. It is truthful, describes conduct rather than identity, respects the unfinished verification and avoids prejudging providers.
Stopping legitimate review because of media attention abandons the integrity mission. Communication and review can both continue responsibly.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider how a public statement about fraud might be heard by a family that receives services lawfully from a provider in the same community. What would you want them to hear?
lessons.action: Use the fictional case or an approved summary to distinguish all flagged cases, completed reviews, confirmed findings and unresolved reviews. Identify what comparison data is missing. Ask the data owner about an appropriate analysis and disclosure controls; do not copy investigation records or infer community-level fraud from the sample.

check.question: Why should oversight teams track the share of flagged cases later confirmed, by group?
check.correct: To identify patterns that warrant closer examination of selection, follow-up and data quality.
wrong: To set quotas for how many providers each group must have reviewed.
To prove that fraud is more common in some communities.
check.feedback: Different confirmation shares can signal a need to examine selection, follow-up and data quality. They do not by themselves establish a false-positive rate, prove unequal treatment or measure fraud across a community. Evaluate the method with appropriate comparison data, documented limits and the responsible staff.

cards.back: An improper payment can result from error or missing documentation; fraud involves intentional deception. Precise labels lead to proportionate responses.
In the GAO framework, the level of fraud risk managers accept after weighing program objectives, such as timely help, against lowering fraud likelihood.

Under 42 CFR 455.23, a credible allegation for which a Medicaid investigation is pending generally requires payment suspension, subject to the rule’s good cause provisions. It is not a final finding of fraud.
A review criterion, such as language or neighborhood, that stands in for race, national origin or another protected trait and can concentrate scrutiny on a community.

Fair procedures for a decision, including applicable notice, an opportunity to respond, an impartial decision-maker and reasons. Timing and hearing rights depend on the benefit or action; provider payment suspensions have distinct rules.

aid.heading: Design proportionate reviews
items: Label each issue precisely: error, improper payment, waste or abuse, or credible fraud indicator.
Match responses to evidence and authority. A tiered approach does not delay a required referral, suspension or other action.
Select for review on conduct and billing patterns, not identity proxies.
Test selection criteria for disparate effects and accuracy before use; refer legal questions to counsel and EOAD.

aid.heading: Protect due process
items: Beneficiary notices and provider-suspension notices have different content and timing rules. Use the requirements for the actual action and state the applicable response or appeal route.
Follow Medicaid advance notice and continuation-of-services rules for people served.
For provider suspensions, follow 42 CFR 455.23 notice content and consider good cause exceptions, including access.
Coordinate continuity planning through authorized channels with relevant counties, Tribal Nations and case managers; protect investigation and client information.

aid.heading: Use data and words carefully
items: Treat every flag as a lead; verify records and consider innocent explanations.
Distinguish completed, confirmed and unresolved reviews. Confirmation shares alone do not establish false-positive rates or community fraud prevalence.
Describe conduct, never communities, in public statements; coordinate with communications and legal.
Report fraud results and access effects together.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Program Integrity
sources.note: Supports the description of DHS program integrity work under the Office of Inspector General, including high-risk service designation, revalidation, enrollment pauses, payment withholds, third-party billing review and resources to help people find care. Specific figures on the page are time-sensitive and are not repeated in the course.

sources.title: U.S. Government Accountability Office — A Framework for Managing Fraud Risks in Federal Programs (GAO-15-593SP)
sources.note: Supports the four components (commit, assess, design and implement, evaluate and adapt), the emphasis on prevention and the discussion of fraud risk tolerance and weighing program objectives. Written for federal managers; applied here by analogy.

sources.title: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services — Medicaid Program Integrity
sources.note: Supports CMS and state program-integrity responsibilities, improper-payment work and the emphasis on data and analytics.

sources.title: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations — 42 CFR 455.23, Suspension of payments in cases of fraud
sources.note: Supports the credible allegation of fraud standard, notice timing and content, and good cause exceptions including jeopardized beneficiary access.

sources.title: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations — 42 CFR part 431, subpart E, Fair Hearings for Applicants and Beneficiaries
sources.note: Supports notice content, advance notice timing and exceptions, the right to a hearing and continuation of services pending a hearing decision.

sources.title: Justia — Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)
sources.note: Supports the due process elements for termination of public assistance described in lesson 3.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Justice — Rescinding Portions of Department of Justice Title VI Regulations, 90 FR 57141 (effective December 10, 2025)
sources.note: Removes the disparate-impact provisions from DOJ Title VI regulations. States that data on disparate outcomes can still help prove intentional discrimination. The rule does not mention language access.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services — Rescinding Portions of the HHS Title VI Regulations, FR Doc. 2026-15000 (effective July 24, 2026)
sources.note: Removes the parallel provisions, including 45 CFR 80.3(b)(2). HHS funds DHS. Formal determinations about its effect belong to counsel and enforcement agencies.

sources.title: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services — Improper Payments Fact Sheet
sources.note: Explains that improper payments and fraud are distinct and that improper-payment estimates are not fraud estimates. Historical payment figures are not used in this course.
